title: Council Post: Why Fashion Supply Chain Traceability Is A Tech Challenge That Begins With AI
text:
Madhava Venkatesh Raghavan is CTO and Co-Founder of TrusTrace, a leading platform for supply chain traceability within fashion and retail.
Call it an example of the government stepping in to do the will of the people. As we speak, the European Commission is working to implement its Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) program, which, when it becomes law, will require companies to calculate and disclose the environmental impact of their products by tracing their origins through supply chains.
Such legislation is a victory for activists and consumer rights groups that have long pushed brands to operate more sustainably, especially fashion brands. According to widely accepted estimates, the fashion industry accounts for as much as 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
PEF will join a slew of regulations worldwide, including California’s Transparency in Supply Chains Act and Germany’s recently passed Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, forcing large companies to get a better handle on their supply chains. This will require technology solutions for supply chain traceability, plus a new way of thinking about sustainability.
Until now, companies have approached sustainability at the corporate level—a top-down push to act more responsibly and market products accordingly. But this is already dated thinking (and, frankly, something most companies already do). What's now required—especially by regulators and consumers—is product-level sustainability.
Gathering sustainability data at the product level means knowing everything about every product and material a company handles. It requires much more granular, accurate data—at scale. Fashion brands command complex, intricate supply chains, including everything from dyes and yarns to fabrics and finished goods. For them, traceability is critical.
The Basics Of Traceability
The ability to precisely trace products and materials through a supply chain can help address many challenges:
• Traceability can lead to greater supply chain visibility, which can help anticipate and avoid the kind of disruptions we’ve seen recently.
• It supports proof of product provenance—knowing exactly where a product and its materials came from.
• It’s the basis for adhering to product claims and proving authenticity. A brand can’t say a sweater is made of 100% organic cotton unless it can trace the origins of that cotton.
• Traceability can result in social accountability, ensuring workers are treated fairly and improving lives in the process.
• And, in the case of the European Commission’s PEF program and similar laws, traceability is required to meet regulatory requirements.
There are certain supply chains in which traceability is well established. The highly regulated pharmaceutical industry, for example, is well experienced in traceability and the automated systems required to establish it.
The fashion industry is nothing like that. Fragmented, sprawling and with little-to-zero supply chain visibility, fashion companies face a daunting task not only in their need to meet new supply chain regulations but also in their efforts to streamline supply chains to support better business outcomes and customer experiences. Striving toward sustainability at the product level requires new thinking.
Product-level responsibility is a technology challenge that will require a full stack of highly scalable, accurate solutions, from artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to IoT tagging that joins the physical and digital worlds and blockchain-powered systems that create a trusted, evidence-based chain of custody. In upcoming articles, I’ll delve into each component of the traceability technology stack, but let’s start with AI—without which we can’t even get started.
AI As The Digital Bridge To Traceability
In my experience working with companies in the fashion industry, most of the data needed to move toward product-level sustainability and supply chain traceability is locked up in documents—paper and electronic. This can include everything from invoices that prove the chain of custody and social audit reports describing a facility’s workplace conditions to chemical tests for specific batches of materials. All this document data could be in different formats and languages.
On top of that, new digital-native data is starting to influence supply chains: satellite images, video data of facilities, employee interviews and testimonials and IoT data from machinery and energy meters. In short, traceability represents a complex data acquisition problem.
While we develop technologies that make existing trade, certification and testing processes natively digital, we need intermediate systems that can help digitize paper trails. This is where AI can come into play—not only because of its OCR-style ability to intelligently ingest data but also its ability to support a system that automatically performs data validation by correlating information from multiple sources to improve the overall data quality.
This digitization of "paper trails" to enable traceability includes the following steps:
• Classification: First, the AI recognizes and identifies a document submitted somewhere in the supply chains and intelligently classifies it as, for example, a purchase order, facility audit or certification.
• Object Extraction And Identification: Based on the document’s classification, AI identifies the key information based on metadata. For example, when processing invoices, the system captures information like buyer, seller, product, quantity and date of delivery. Similarly, digitizing a social audit might involve capturing parameters related to working conditions, fair wages, diversity and more.
• Data Validation And Linking: Once the corresponding objects are extracted from the supporting documents, the data is validated and linked to other data within existing enterprise systems to allow companies to act on it, whether for forecasting, analytics, regulatory reporting or other requirements.
When supply chain traceability data is all digital, AI and machine learning can have ongoing roles. Supply chains are so complex and the available data so vast that AI will be needed for companies to act fast, such as when one partner's sustainability can’t meet a brand’s standards and the supply chain must adapt and reconfigure through other partners to remain in compliance.
As the European Commission’s PEF program demonstrates, it soon won’t be enough for brands to simply prove sustainability; they’ll have to calculate in near real time how sustainable their products are by intelligently tracing their combined materials. This is the textbook definition of product-level responsibility.
Many fashion brands were already committed to sustainability and social responsibility before the world’s legislators became involved. That corporate commitment must now permeate brands at the product level. It’s a big challenge but AI is one way to meet it.

title: The ex-Google researcher staring down Big Tech
text:
The ex-Google researcher staring down Big Tech
With help from Rishika Dugyala and Teresa Wiltz
What up Recast family! Moderna seeks FDA authorization for a second booster for adults, an American civilian is killed in a Russian assault in Ukraine, and a Russian court extends WNBA star Brittney Griner’s detention until at least May. Today, we’re kicking things off with a thought leader in ethical issues in artificial intelligence.
Timnit Gebru is a renowned computer scientist and leading expert on the racial bias of facial recognition tools.
She is also among the 40 people and organizations named to The Recast Power List we debuted last week. She made the list for her whistleblowing efforts to root out the harm technology can have on marginalized groups — not to mention her advocacy of greater diversity and inclusion within Silicon Valley.
Her controversial firing from Google in late 2020 jolted the tech industry. She says her termination was over academic research she co-wrote spelling out the dangers of some of the AI technology that is used to power Google’s search engines.
“Of course, all of it — in my view — was related to the fact that I am a Black woman,” she said when asked if race played a role in her firing during my POLITICO Live interview with her this week.
(In an email to Google employees, Jeff Dean, the head of Google AI, said Gebru’s paper didn’t “meet our bar for publication” and that Gebru required “that a number of conditions be met in order for her to continue working at Google. … We accept and respect her decision to resign from Google.”)
Gebru is now charting a path of her own through her own organization, Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (DAIR). It aims to raise awareness about the harm AI technologies can cause while also pushing tech giants and lawmakers for greater oversight and accountability.
Gebru, who was born in Ethiopia to Eritrean parents, is committed to disseminating DAIR’s research among communities impacted by harmful AI, particularly those in Africa.
We chop it up about her time at Google, what more lawmakers could be doing in their oversight of big tech firms and if she sees a difference in how the media covers women of color whistleblowers in tech versus their white counterparts.
◆◆◆
This interview has been adapted from a Politico Live event and edited for length and clarity.
THE RECAST: How much do you think the scrutiny you received at Google was tied to your identity as a woman of color challenging the status quo and challenging authority?
GEBRU: All of it. I mean, where do I even start?
So, the paper that we wrote, first of all, was from the perspective of people in marginalized groups. There were about seven authors … from the LGBTQ+ community, Latinos, Black people, women, members of the indigenous communities. We also had about four or five continents represented. So in this case, the conversation about large language models that we had was from that perspective.
And so [Google managers aren’t ] used to hearing people express our opinions about potential harmful technology from our perspective.
I had been having so many issues at Google during my two years there. I started talking about the issues that I saw, especially with respect to women and Black people and how they were being treated. I started facing resistance right away. The latest episode that got me fired was just one of a string of issues that I was facing there.
Every week, we sit down with diverse and influential characters who are shaking up politics.
Who should we profile next? Let us know. Email us at [email protected].
THE RECAST: We didn't see the same kind of groundswell of support that we saw for, say, Frances Haugen, the Facebook whistleblower, who is a white woman. Haugen testified before Congress alleging Facebook magnifies hate and misinformation on its platform and had this trove of documents that she said backed up her claim.
What do you make of the difference between the support that Haugen received and what you received from mainstream media?
GEBRU: First of all, I want to say I am happy that she got that support. I am happy that she was able to have her voice heard in [mainstream outlets] like “60 Minutes.” I hope that it results in tangible change.
That being said, I mean, we do know that Black women are not heard, right? When we speak up, we're “angry” — that's how we are characterized. And I'm not quite sure what kind of backlash she faced, but the backlash I faced was huge.
I still have people talking about how my work was “subpar.”
And in terms of “60 Minutes,” there was even an episode on face recognition and wrongful arrests of people based on flawed technology. If I had to name one person who is a pioneer in this space, it's Joy Buolamwini. And they were talking about her work, basically, and they had a white man discuss her work.
So in short, it's no secret how we are treated when we speak up as Black women.
I'm grateful that Francis Haugen did speak up. Hopefully, the public is getting some of the message that we have to rein in these large tech companies. They have too much power, and they're doing a lot of harmful things without any sort of checks and balances or oversight on them.
[Editor’s Note: Buolamwini says she spoke with “60 Minutes” producers for hours for their May 2021 story on facial recognition, including providing research recommendations and people to interview. In a statement, CBS said while they didn’t interview her on camera “she was an important part of the research we did due to her work in this field.”]
THE RECAST: President Biden ran on a platform promising to root out inequities in federal agencies and programs. Has his administration done enough to tackle the issue of discriminatory AI?
GEBRU: I'm glad to see that some initiatives have started. I like that the Office Of Science And Technology Policy (OSTP), for instance, is filled with people I respect, like Alondra Nelson, who is now its head.
My biggest comment on this is that a lot of tech companies — all tech companies — actually, don't have to do any sort of test to prove that they're not putting out harmful products.
So, we were talking about face recognition a long time ago and … we don't have a federal bill. We even have all of these segments of the government using it: law enforcement and you saw ID.me with the IRS.
So the issue is we are looking to the government to regulate this technology and have some sort of oversight, but then we're also seeing the government using this unregulated harmful technology.
This is an issue for me.
I'd like to see the federal government come up with regulation, but also look at itself and what kinds of technology that it is using as well.
THE RECAST: Where do you anticipate this action coming from? I see lawmakers relish the fact that they can bring big tech heads in and grill them on their technologies. But when it comes to passing oversight laws, there’s little appetite for getting that legislation across the finish line.
GEBRU: There absolutely needs to be grassroots pressure.
But what I'm trying to say is that the grassroots people are very under-resourced and overburdened. They're constantly trying to prove harm.
The problem is that these tech companies have so many resources. They have people all day whose jobs are to lobby members of Congress and senators and other legislators, even internationally in the EU, etc.
People like me, I try to talk to as many people as I can in the government. But I don't have the resources or time to do this all day. So, that action has to come from everybody. I think everybody has a role to play.
THE RECAST: Well, let's talk DAIR. A lot of organizations say they want to kind of influence tech practices from the outside. But, as you mentioned, it’s a resource issue. What makes DAIR distinct?
GEBRU: I really do believe in the phrase: power to the people. I think that people have power and we can exercise that power.
So, with DAIR, that is kind of the underlying philosophy that we have. We know we're not going to have the unlimited money that Google has, or even the military has.
Historically, how AI research has been developed, there's been two major sources of funding: One is something to do with warfare, like DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency). If you look at even self-driving cars, the Robo cops, etc., machine translation has roots in the Cold War. So it's either that, or these large corporations trying to maximize profit.
At DAIR, … we make sure that the money that we're getting, at least, is not motivated by either of these two goals. And, we want to be able to stop the harms of AI without being fired from places when we try to educate our community about the potential harms of AI.
We want to do the development and the research in a way that will benefit our communities. And, when we see existing technology that's harming our communities, we want to be able to work on helping stop that technology without being persecuted.
THE RECAST: Some of the push you're trying to do with DAIR is work with countries in Africa that can help kind of illuminate these problems with AI or find some potential solutions that could be applied globally?
GEBRU: Absolutely, we have to have an international view.
I am of Eritrean descent. I was born and raised in Ethiopia. What has been happening in Ethiopia?
There has been a war with rape used as a weapon of war, starvation used as a weapon of war, unspeakable horrors that you can imagine. An estimated 500,000 people dead in the last 16 months in a region of maybe 6 million people.
I have not heard a single news story about it. Eritrea has one of the highest refugees per capita and what happens to them? They get drowned in the Mediterranean. And so, there's all sorts of tech involved in this kind of stuff, too, that we don't have time to talk about right now.
These tech companies are concentrated in the U.S., that are impacting the entire world, but the entire world doesn't have the ability to impact them. So with DAIR, that's what we're hoping to do. I also don't want to contribute to the brain drain. If someone in an African country wants to work at DAIR, I don't want them to have to leave that community and then have to move to Silicon Valley or something like that. I want them to enrich their own communities. So, that is a part of the philosophy of DAIR as well.
THE RECAST: My final question here, what advice do you have for those who aspire to do what you are doing in shaking up these power dynamics in the tech industry?
GEBRU: Just remember: power to the people. People have power.
I think we forget how much power people have when they work collectively and when they have collective advocacy, when they do collective organizing. So, when you're thinking about what to do and what to change, don't think about it just as yourself, you as an individual.
I always think about myself in the context of the tech organizing movement. There are a lot of people who play a lot of roles. There are a lot of people behind the scenes, whose names you don't know about, that I talk to all the time. They’re part of this movement [too].
So I always ask people to think about where you think you might fit in this movement. How you can build coalitions and advocacy, and solidarity. You advocate on someone else's behalf. Someone else advocates on your behalf. And that's kind of what creates change.
